name: Bizarreness effect
statement: Sentences describing implausible scenes are freely recalled better than ordinary ones, but only when both kinds sit in the same study list.
meaning: The standard test uses sentences carrying three capitalised target nouns. A common sentence reads 'The DOG chased the BICYCLE down the STREET' and its bizarre counterpart reads 'The DOG rode the BICYCLE down the STREET'. Participants read and rate each sentence, work through a filler task, then write down the target nouns with no cues. Bizarre sentences win, and the conditions under which they win are narrow. Both kinds have to be studied in one list, the test has to be free recall rather than cued recall, and the sentences have to be simple. In one line of work the participant also has to be unaware that memory will be tested. Scoring matters as well. The gain appears as access to a greater number of sentences, not as more nouns recovered from each sentence recalled.

origin.who: Mark A. McDaniel and Gilles O. Einstein
origin.where: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
origin.note: The advice is far older than the finding. Besken and Mulligan trace it to the Ad Herennium, which they date at 90 BCE, by way of Yates, and to modern memory-training manuals. Riefer and Rouder write that most early experimental work found bizarre imagery no more memorable than common imagery and sometimes worse, naming Wollen, Weber and Lowry, Cox and Wollen, and Bergfeld, Choate and Kroll. What the 1986 paper contributed was the boundary, as Burns, Geraci and colleagues and Robinson-Riegler and McDaniel all describe it: the advantage holds when bizarre and common sentences are mixed in one list, and not when a list is pure. The paper itself was not obtained, and the limits field says where the search looked.

evidence: Riefer and Rouder ran three experiments on 95 students at the University of California, Irvine, 33 in the first, 32 in the second and 30 in the third. Each participant saw 12 sentences, six of them randomly assigned to bizarre form, imagined each one and rated its vividness, then took a surprise free-recall test followed by a cued-recall test. Free recall of noun pairs ran .58 bizarre against .47 common in the first experiment, t(32) = 2.37, and .62 against .51 in the third, t(29) = 2.82. The second gave .59 against .54 and was not reliable, t(31) = 1.17. Cued recall differed in none of the three. Their multinomial model put the benefit in retrieval rather than storage. Bizarre sentences were also rated less vivid than common ones in all three experiments, on an analysis over the 12 sentences rather than over subjects. Burns tested whether the participant has to be caught unawares, using McDaniel and Einstein's own sentences with 24 people per condition in one experiment and 16 in the other. Under incidental instructions his participants accessed 3.96 bizarre sentences against 2.42 common ones; under intentional instructions the same comparison gave 3.71 against 3.50, F < 1. Items recalled per sentence went the other way in his first experiment, 2.39 for bizarre sentences against 2.65 for common ones, F(1,46) = 5.83. Geraci, McDaniel, Miller and Hughes separated study from test with 192 Texas A&M students, 96 in each recall condition. Each person studied eight common sentences in one room under one cover story and eight bizarre sentences in another room on a different floor under another, so both lists were pure. Recall was then either of both sets together or of each set separately. Together, bizarre nouns came back at .38 and common nouns at .28, F(1, 190) = 18.17. Separately, the figures were .34 and .33, with F < 1 and a posterior probability of .91 for the null.

replication.headline: Besken and Mulligan obtained the effect on sentence access in all four of their experiments, and their single-paper meta-analysis puts that advantage at .31, 95% CI .21 to .42.
replication.detail: The four experiments were designed to attack the imagery explanation, not to test whether the effect exists, which makes them a clean check on it. Mixed lists of bizarre and common sentences were studied under a concurrent visuospatial load or without one, by 36, 60, 32 and 32 undergraduates. The first experiment ran three groups rather than two, and its auditory control condition produced no bizarreness effect on either measure, both ts < 1. Sentence access carried the effect in all four experiments. Noun recall carried it in the first three and fell short in the fourth, F(1, 30) = 3.41, p = .075, with the difference in the predicted direction. The single-paper meta-analysis, run by the McShane and Böckenholt procedure, gives a main effect of sentence type of .31 with a 95% interval of .21 to .42 for sentence access and .20 with an interval of .09 to .31 for noun recall, both in proportion units. The pooled interaction with distraction was not significant for sentence access, F(1, 158) = 1.22, or for noun recall, F(1, 158) = 2.31, and the Bayes factors favouring the null over the imagery prediction were 11.49 and 13.86. Any numerical trend ran opposite to the imagery account. Replication of the effect is therefore secure inside the mixed-list free-recall paradigm and is not secure outside it. Geraci and colleagues found nothing when the two sentence types were recalled separately, and Riefer and Rouder found nothing in cued recall in three experiments.

study.cite: Besken, M., & Mulligan, N. W. (2022). The bizarreness effect and visual imagery: No impact of concurrent visuo-spatial distractor tasks indicates little role for visual imagery. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 48(9), 1281-1295.

limits: No meta-analysis of the bizarreness literature as a whole was located. Crossref, Europe PMC, OSF Preprints, Semantic Scholar and general web search were tried on 17 August 2026, and what came back was single experiments, review chapters and one single-paper meta-analysis covering four experiments by the same authors. McDaniel and Einstein's 1986 paper was not obtained. Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and PsycNet were tried on 17 August 2026, all record it as closed, and ResearchGate returned 403 for the author copy. Its design and its effect sizes are reported as Besken and Mulligan describe them, which is average within-subject effect sizes of dz = .86 for noun recall and dz = .93 for sentence access in the mixed-list imagery conditions, quoted there to support a post-hoc power calculation. Those figures are kept out of the structured fields for that reason. Einstein, McDaniel and Lackey's 1989 paper is closed at Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar on the same day and was not read. Robinson-Riegler and McDaniel were read. Their four experiments find that complex sentences carry a mnemonic benefit of their own, that the benefit sits in sentence access, and that its retrieval cues outshine whatever cue bizarreness supplies, which confines the effect to what they call an impoverished encoding context of simple unelaborated sentences. Cued recall is the clearest failure: Riefer and Rouder obtained no difference in any of three experiments. Macias and Persaud took the question to colour, testing memory for object colours with a four-alternative recognition task immediately and again three days later. Neither study found an advantage for expectation-incongruent colours, and both found a long-term advantage running the other way, to congruent items. Burns's own summary is that the effect needs mixed lists, free recall, low-complexity sentences and an unsuspecting participant, and that this leaves the value of bizarre imagery as a mnemonic technique open to doubt. The same venues on the same day turned up no test of the effect in advertising or interface design.
misreadings: The mnemonists have it backwards on Burns's evidence, with his own caveat attached. He found the advantage under incidental instructions and lost it under intentional ones, which is the condition anybody deliberately using the technique is in. He then states that his point is not whether the effect can be produced under intentional learning, and names Wollen and Cox and Hirshman, Whelley and Palij as having produced it that way. Surprise is not the mechanism. McDaniel, Einstein, DeLosh, May and Brady report that manipulations built to raise or lower the surprise a bizarre sentence provokes had little effect on recall, contrary to expectation-violation theory, and their title says so. Visual imagery is not the mechanism either, on the current evidence. Three separate visuospatial distractor tasks left the effect intact in Besken and Mulligan's experiments, and bizarre sentences are rated less vivid than common ones, not more. The relation to the von Restorff effect is close and is not identity. Both need a mixed list, and Geraci and colleagues place bizarreness alongside orthographic distinctiveness as effects that vanish in pure lists. The isolation paradigm sets one item against a list of many that are alike, so rarity is built into it by definition. The bizarreness paradigm splits the list roughly in half, and McDaniel and colleagues found in their first experiment that mixing itself, rather than the small number of bizarre sentences usually used, decided whether the effect appeared. Where the two fail is usually quoted flat, and it is not flat. Kamp and colleagues write that there is rarely an isolation effect for recognition, and their six experiments split three and three. The first three found a free recall advantage but no recognition advantage unless recall was tested first. Three more, with more observations per subject and the test order controlled, produced von Restorff effects for both recognition and source memory. Zhao, Zimmer, Zheng and Fu report that bizarreness improved associative recognition of verb-object pairs after a verbal task and not after a subject-performed task. Encoding is not where the work happens, on Geraci and colleagues' reading of their own data. They had participants study pure lists in separate rooms and got the effect back by asking for both sets at once, which locates the advantage at retrieval, and Riefer and Rouder's model had already put it in retrieval rather than storage. They add that the result does not preclude extra encoding for bizarre sentences, and their study-order interaction, which they read as recency, is the reason to leave that open.
